title: Remembrance And Peace, Reported From Two Sources
slot: Religious Education & Ethics (AQA GCSE Religious Studies)
objective: Report what two approved sources say about remembrance and peace, compare them using the frame, and name one shared point and one difference without stating your own view.

blocks.text: LAUNCH · Humanities · Week 6. Religious Education and Ethics. Remembrance And Peace, Reported From Two Sources.
Objective: report what two approved sources say about remembrance and peace, compare them using the frame, and name one shared point and one difference.
Success evidence: two reports, each naming its source, plus one shared point and one difference.
Every quotation comes from the approved source sheet. You report what a source teaches. You are not asked what you believe, and never about your family.
40 minutes. Offline.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Source sheets and frames out before pupils sit. A pupil writing before the frame arrives will write an opinion.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil offers what they or their family believe, say that the sheet is what we report today, and move to the next source. Do not follow it up.

blocks.text: Report and agree are different jobs
Remembrance is an act. Peace is an idea. Traditions hold both, and not in the same way.
Your job today is to report. Reporting means saying what a source teaches.
Agreeing means saying you think it is true. We never ask that.
Nor does the exam. It asks what a tradition teaches.
So every sentence starts on the sheet, not in your head.
Say the report-and-agree rule once and leave it on the board. It is the guard the whole lesson rests on.
You need the source sheet, the frame and a pencil.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Show both answers side by side. Do not say which is better; let the group find the checkable one.

blocks.text: Two answers on the same silence
Answer A says the two-minute silence is moving and everyone should keep it. It scores nothing.
Answer B says source one describes the silence as shared respect for the dead.
Answer B names a source. Answer A names a feeling.
Read both. Ask which one an examiner could check against the sheet.
Only one can be checked. That is the whole difference.

items: 1 · name the source you are using.
2 · report what it teaches in your own words.
3 · set it beside the second source.
4 · label the point as shared or different.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Model source one fully, then stop and let the group build the report for source two.

blocks.text: One source reported, then the second
I take source one, a Christian statement on remembrance from the sheet.
I write: source one teaches that remembering the dead is a duty of respect.
That sentence reports. It does not say whether I find it moving.
Now source two, a Muslim statement on peace.
I write: source two teaches that peace begins when a person chooses not to return harm.

blocks.caption: The source number travels with the sentence to the end
blocks.title: From source to labelled comparison
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: name the source, report what it teaches, compare it with the second, label the point

blocks.text: Two reports, two sources named. Now they can be compared.
The compare step is one sentence. Both sources treat peace as something the living must act for.
Stop visibly after the second report and say why. Pupils drift into judgement in the third sentence, not the first.
Notice what I never wrote. I never wrote that one source is better.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Cards sorted first, hands down. Nobody speaks until every table has finished the sort.

blocks.text: Sort the cards, then match them
Six statement cards sit on your table. Sort them into reports and opinions.
A report says what a source teaches. An opinion says what a person thinks.
Then match each report card to the source it came from, one or two.
Two cards are hard. They report a source, then add an opinion.
Put those in a third pile. Say where the opinion starts.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Source sheet stays face up beside the frame. The shared point is found on the page, never from memory.

blocks.text: Naming shared ground without flattening it
The easy mistake is to write that all religions want peace, then stop.
It is too wide to mark. You could write it without reading a source.
A shared point must be narrow enough to point at on the sheet.
So I write: both sources place the duty on the living, not on the dead.

blocks.caption: Same reading of the same sheet, and only one carries a source
blocks.title: Reported against judged
blocks.alt: Two boxes compared: a reported sentence keeps its source number, a judged one drops it

blocks.text: The second column fails because it removes the source.
With the source gone, an examiner has nothing to credit.

items: 1 · a shared point names something both sources say.
2 · a difference keeps each tradition's own wording.
3 · both sentences carry a source number.
4 · neither sentence says who is right.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Pair by table. Two minutes each way, timed out loud, sheets swapped not read aloud.

blocks.text: Underline the reporting verb
Work in twos. Swap sheets and read your partner's reports silently.
Underline the reporting verb in each one. Teaches, describes, states, calls.
If think, feel or believe is used about the writer, ring it.
That word has moved the sentence from report to opinion.
Hand it back and say which word you ringed.
Then swap back and check yours.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Scribe exactly. Do not repair a pupil's opinion into a report; mark it as opinion and let them change the verb.
stages.data-ta2: A pupil who cannot choose a shared point may point at a line on the sheet. Record that line as the choice.

blocks.text: Two reports, one shared point, one difference
Work on your own, using the frame and the source sheet.
Write one report for source one and one report for source two.
Name the source in each. Use a reporting verb in each.
Then write one sentence naming a point they share, narrow enough to point at.
Then write one sentence naming a difference, in each tradition's own words.

items: Supported · one report with its source named, using the frame.
Standard · two reports, plus a shared point and a difference, each carrying a source.
Stretch · as Standard, and name the word that would turn your shared point into an opinion.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: The named adult reads it back word for word and says reported or judged. No paraphrase, no praise.

blocks.text: Read one report to an adult
Read one report to the adult at your table.
They read it back and say whether it reported or judged.
If it judged, change the verb rather than the whole sentence.
Then choose what happens next. Keep it, rewrite the second report, or add a third source.
Write that choice on the sheet with today's date before you leave.

sections: The shared point and the difference
print.intro: Use the frame for both sources. Leave a box blank rather than filling it with what you think about the source.
focusRows: Two reports, each naming its source and using a reporting verb
One shared point narrow enough to point at on the sheet
One difference written in each tradition's own words
tiers: Write one report with its source named, using the frame.
Write two reports, then a shared point and a difference, each carrying a source.
As Standard, and name the word that would turn your shared point into an opinion.
checks: Each report names a source from the approved sheet.
Each report uses a reporting verb, not think, feel or believe.
The shared point can be traced to a line on the sheet.
No sentence states whether the pupil agrees with either source.
